what_this_is: Fixed answers every conformant KERI implementation must reproduce byte for byte. Generated from keripy, which the KERI implementations table lists at 100% spec compliance. Regenerate rather than edit: a hand-edited expectation is a belief, not a reference.
how_to_use: Run every implementation against every case. raw_b64 is the authoritative serialisation — the readable event is for humans and its key order is not the order that was signed.

cases.why: CESR codes are normative. An implementation that emits a different prefix is producing values no other implementation can read.

The simplest identity there is. If this one disagrees, nothing else can agree. Single-key inception uses basic derivation: the identifier is the key itself (D…), not a digest — an implementation that always digests produces identities nobody recognises.

Multi-key inception uses self-addressing derivation: the identifier is a digest of the event (E…), equal to the SAID. An implementation that uses basic derivation here, or that formats the threshold as a number rather than the string '1', produces an identity no peer will recognise.

Multi-key inception uses self-addressing derivation: the identifier is a digest of the event (E…), equal to the SAID. An implementation that uses basic derivation here, or that formats the threshold as a number rather than the string '2', produces an identity no peer will recognise.

Multi-key inception uses self-addressing derivation: the identifier is a digest of the event (E…), equal to the SAID. An implementation that uses basic derivation here, or that formats the threshold as a number rather than the string '3', produces an identity no peer will recognise.
Fractional thresholds are serialised as a list of strings, not a single integer. An implementation that only knows integer thresholds will either refuse a valid event or produce a different identity.
A single witness is part of the identifier. An implementation that omits witnesses, or that uses transferable keys as witnesses, disagrees with every peer.
Witnesses and the threshold of acceptable duplicity (toad) are part of the identifier. Different toad values are different identities even with the same witness list.
Witnesses and the threshold of acceptable duplicity (toad) are part of the identifier. Different toad values are different identities even with the same witness list.
Witnesses and the threshold of acceptable duplicity (toad) are part of the identifier. Different toad values are different identities even with the same witness list.
Larger witness sets still enter the digest. An implementation that truncates the list or reorders it produces a different identity.
Larger witness sets still enter the digest. An implementation that truncates the list or reorders it produces a different identity.
An anchored seal changes the identifier, which is the whole point of anchoring. An implementation that drops or reorders seals produces a different identity.
Several seals are ordered: swapping them changes the identifier. An implementation that sorts seals, or collapses them, is not interoperable.
Seal field order is part of the signed bytes. Alphabetical sorting of seal keys produces a different identifier than the order the event was written in.
A seal written d-then-i-then-s is a different event from one written i-s-d. An implementation that puts seals through a hash map silently changes every anchored identity.
A rotation must carry the key the previous event committed to, and must chain to that event by digest. Both are places an implementation can quietly differ.

Changing the threshold is itself a commitment recorded in the event. An implementation that leaves the old threshold in place, or encodes the new one as a number rather than a string, disagrees with every peer about who may sign next.

Adding a witness is recorded as ba (backers add). An implementation that rewrites the full witness list instead of emitting the delta, or that omits the new toad, produces a rotation no peer will accept.
Removing a witness is recorded as br (backers remove). An implementation that drops a witness without emitting br has not said what it thinks it said.
Cuts and adds in the same rotation are ordered fields of one event. Swapping them, or applying them in the wrong order to reconstruct the witness set, yields a different next state.

A rotation can anchor data the same way an interaction can. Dropping the seal, or serialising it differently, changes the event digest and breaks the chain for anyone verifying against the real history.

Each rotation digests the previous event. An implementation that always points at the inception, or that mis-encodes the sequence number as it grows past single digits (sn=1), cannot be followed by anyone else.

Each rotation digests the previous event. An implementation that always points at the inception, or that mis-encodes the sequence number as it grows past single digits (sn=2), cannot be followed by anyone else.

Each rotation digests the previous event. An implementation that always points at the inception, or that mis-encodes the sequence number as it grows past single digits (sn=3), cannot be followed by anyone else.

An interaction with an empty seal list is still a real event with a real digest. An implementation that omits the 'a' field entirely, rather than emitting an empty array, produces bytes no peer will verify.
Interaction events are how a credential is anchored into a key history, so their serialisation decides whether an issuance can be verified elsewhere.
Multiple seals are ordered. Sorting them, or hashing them as a set, changes the event digest and makes the anchor unverifiable.
Seal field order is part of the signed bytes on interaction events too. A hash-map serialiser turns a valid anchor into a different event.
Sequence numbers are lowercase hex strings without a 0x prefix. sn=10 serialises as 'a'. An implementation that uses decimal, uppercase, or padded hex produces an event nobody else can chain from.
Sequence numbers are lowercase hex strings without a 0x prefix. sn=16 serialises as '10'. An implementation that uses decimal, uppercase, or padded hex produces an event nobody else can chain from.
Sequence numbers are lowercase hex strings without a 0x prefix. sn=255 serialises as 'ff'. An implementation that uses decimal, uppercase, or padded hex produces an event nobody else can chain from.
Sequence numbers are lowercase hex strings without a 0x prefix. sn=256 serialises as '100'. An implementation that uses decimal, uppercase, or padded hex produces an event nobody else can chain from.
The delegator is an ordinary identifier. Recorded so a chain that includes a delegated identifier has the root event the rest of the chain points at.
A delegated inception (dip) names its delegator in di and uses self-addressing derivation. An implementation that emits an ordinary icp, or that omits di, has not created a delegated identifier.
Delegation is only complete when the delegator anchors the dip. The seal must carry the delegated identifier, its sequence number, and its SAID — any other shape is not a delegation anchor.

A delegated rotation (drt) is not an ordinary rot: the ilk differs, and acceptance still depends on the delegator's authority. Emitting rot here produces an event no peer treating this as delegated will accept.

A credential's schema SAID is part of what a verifier checks offline. An implementation that recomputes a different SAID for the same schema rejects every credential issued against it, or accepts forged ones.

cases.why: A credential registry is itself a self-addressing identifier. An implementation that formats the registry inception differently produces a registry no issued credential will name, so every issuance fails to bind.

A registry-backed credential names its registry in ri, and its own SAID is a digest of its canonical bytes. A verifier offline must recompute that SAID exactly; any other serialisation means the credential cannot be checked.
Not every credential is registry-backed. Omitting ri is part of the serialisation: inventing a registry field, or requiring one, produces a different SAID and a credential no peer recognises.

Issuance is a TEL event whose identifier is the credential's SAID. An implementation that digests the wrong fields, or that points ri at the issuer rather than the registry, cannot be reconciled with any peer's TEL.

A registry issuance is only bound to the issuer when the issuer anchors it. The seal carries the registry, the TEL sequence number and the iss SAID — any other shape is not an issuance anchor and will not verify offline.

An edge chains one credential to another. The edge is inside the SAID, so dropping it, reordering it, or changing the nested schema reference produces a different credential that no longer proves the link.

Rules travel inside the credential and enter its SAID. An implementation that strips the rules section, or that serialises it differently, produces a credential whose digest no longer matches what was issued.

A privacy-preserving credential carries a salt (u) at the top level and in the subject. That salt is part of the SAID. An implementation that omits it, or that generates a fresh one on read, cannot verify a credential it did not itself issue — and selective disclosure depends on this form.

Revocation is a TEL event that chains to the issuance by digest. An implementation that does not require that link, or that leaves the credential SAID pointing at a still-issued state, accepts revoked credentials as valid.

A verifier must know the TEL state of a credential: issued, then revoked. Capturing both events and their order is what makes an offline check decide correctly rather than assume 'present means valid'.

A receipt names the event it covers by digest and sequence number. An implementation that points a receipt at the wrong digest is not covering the event it thinks it is, and peers will not count it toward the toad.

A single witness receipt is a stream: the receipt event plus a non-transferable couple (witness identifier + cigar). Witnesses are non-transferable, so the identifier IS the verifying key — capture enough that a checker holding only the key event can verify the cigar.
Several witnesses sign the same event. The couples are ordered in the attachment; an implementation that drops one, reorders them, or deduplicates by key changes whether the toad is met.

The toad is met when enough designated witnesses have signed. An implementation that miscounts, or that counts signatures from keys not in the witness list, accepts events that are not fully witnessed.
One receipt against a toad of two is not enough. Treating it as met lets an event proceed without the witness protection the identity committed to at inception.
A receipt whose signature does not verify must be refused. Accepting it counts a witness vote that was never cast, and the toad becomes meaningless.

cases.why: Only witnesses named at establishment may contribute to the toad. A receipt from anyone else must be refused — otherwise an attacker supplies as many 'witnesses' as they need.

input.because: the signing identifier is not in the event's witness list

expect.because: the signing identifier is not in the event's witness list

cases.why: Receipts are checked against a specific event. Capturing the event bytes and the controller signature together is what lets a later implementation verify 'this is the event, this is who ran it, these are the witnesses' without inventing any of the three.

Events travel with their controller signature attached in a counted CESR stream. An implementation that can build events but cannot parse the attachment cannot accept anything that arrives on the wire.
A multi-key identity attaches one indexed signature per signing key. Losing the index, reordering the sigers, or requiring all keys when the threshold is 2-of-3 breaks every multi-sig exchange.

A fully witnessed message carries the controller signature group and the non-transferable receipt couples in one stream. The counter codes that introduce each group (-A, -C) are how a parser knows what follows; getting them wrong makes the rest of the stream unreadable.
Attachment groups are introduced by fixed CESR counter codes. An implementation that invents its own introducers cannot exchange signed events with any other KERI implementation.
A truncated CESR stream must be refused. Accepting a partial attachment treats a missing signature as present, or fails later in a way that looks like a different bug.

cases.why: Single-key inception uses basic derivation: the identifier is the public key (D…), not the event digest. An implementation that always sets aid = said breaks every single-key identity that already exists.
Multi-key inception uses self-addressing derivation: the identifier IS the digest of the event. An implementation where these differ has not made a multi-key identity.
Kept for continuity with the first vector file. For this multi-key style event the aid equals the said; for single-key basic derivation it does not — see property/single-key-aid-is-the-key.
An event whose contents do not digest to the identifier it claims must be refused. Accepting it would let a forged event borrow a real identity, which is what the digest exists to prevent.

cases.why: A rotation must present a key the previous establishment event committed to via its next-key digests. Accepting any other key lets an attacker take over the identifier without holding the committed material.
